newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein to have new talks with British officials.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein to have new talks with British officials.

text.p: Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), will meet British officials on Wednesday for the first time since republican guerrillas ended a truce in February 1996, political sources said on Tuesday.

They said Sinn Fein politicians and British civil servants would hold talks in Belfast after Britain's new prime minister Tony Blair eased a ban on contacts last week in a bid to galvanise stalled efforts to bring peace to Northern Ireland.
On the eve of the talks, Britain was reported to have decided to repatriate two convicted Catholic republican prisoners from English jails to a Northern Ireland prison.
Sinn Fein has demanded repatriation and early releases for what it calls "political prisoners" as evidence of British good faith in reviving the province's shattered peace process.

The disclosure of the imminent transfer of Danny McNamee and Liam McCotter, serving sentences for explosives offences, was made by Seamus Mallon, deputy leader of the main Catholic-backed moderate Social Democratic and Labour Party.
He told Reuters he had been informed of it by the British government, and that "it can only be of benefit to the political process here and the search for peace."

Sinn Fein vice-president Pat Doherty said he welcomed the move. "Under British law, all of the Irish republican political prisoners in Britain should have been moved long ago," he said in a statement.

An outlawed pro-British Protestant militia group earlier warned Blair against watering down conditions for Sinn Fein's entry to multi-party peace talks on the future of the British-ruled province, which are due to resume on June 3.
The Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) said London must not "distort the (peace) process to the advantage of republicans" by relaxing a demand for a new, full IRA ceasefire.
"If the IRA fail to bring their campaign to an end they run the risk of pulling our society back into bloody conflict," the UFF said in a statement to a media outlet in Belfast.
Sinn Fein, which won two seats in the British parliament at the May 1 election, is banned from the peace negotiations until the IRA renews its ceasefire.
The IRA, fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland and unite the province with the Irish Republic, broke a 17-month truce in February last year with a series of bombs.

The UFF and other extremist groups, which have killed nationalist Roman Catholics in a campaign to thwart the IRA, have operated a ceasefire since October 1994. But it has become increasingly shaky in recent months because of IRA violence.

Sinn Fein's four-person delegation to a meeting with British officials will be led by Martin McGuinness, its chief negotiator who won a seat in the British parliament along with party president Gerry Adams.
Adams called on Tuesday for a British promise of direct entry to peace talks for Sinn Fein if the IRA abandoned violence.
Blair pledged the province would remain part of the United Kingdom as long as a majority in the province supported it.
